summary:
Gender nonconformity is itself criminalised in Sudan. Article 152 of the Penal Code prohibits wearing clothing of the opposite sex, and the provision addresses gender presentation rather than sexual conduct. A trans visitor whose appearance is read as incongruent with the sex recorded on their documents falls within its scope regardless of any other behaviour.

Sodomy is criminalised under Article 148 of the Criminal Act of 1991, as amended in 2009. The offence is defined as anal sex, whether between people of the same sex or of different sexes, and applies to men and women alike. Penalties set by the amendment adopted by the Transitional Sovereignty Council on 9 July 2020 are up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence, up to seven years for a second, and life imprisonment for a third. The same amendment abolished the death penalty for anal sex and the 100 lashes previously imposed for same-sex intimacy; before that repeal, capital punishment was available for a third offence. No executions for sodomy were documented before the repeal, and in 2011 there were no reports of the antisodomy provision being applied.

Sudan has no legal gender recognition. Gender-affirming healthcare is legally constrained, and state reliance on Sunni fatwas blocks transition. The armed conflict has further restricted access to care.

State violence against LGBTQIA+ people is documented, including extrajudicial killings and torture, alongside official discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Vigilantes have targeted suspected gay men and lesbians for violent abuse, and public demonstrations against homosexuality have taken place. Few people are prepared to speak openly about LGBT issues. In the 2019 Arab Barometer Survey, 17 per cent of Sudanese respondents said homosexuality is acceptable; no tolerance figure specific to transgender people is available.

The US State Department's 2010 human rights report for Sudan recorded criminalisation under Article 148 with flogging and capital punishment available, and documented extrajudicial killings and torture under the Bashir government.
tangentialFactors:
Sudan has voted against every UN resolution supportive of LGBTQ rights and in February 2011 supported a No Action Motion, carried 9-7, that prevented a vote on consultative status for an LGBTQ organisation at the UN Economic and Social Council.

Sudanese LGBTQ activists described the July 2020 amendment as a first step and said it fell short of their goal of decriminalising gay sexual activity altogether.

Research published in 2014 with the Nile Valley LGBTQI organisation Bedayaa recorded daily struggles, discrimination and violence against LGBTQI people rooted in societal gender and sexual norms.
localsOnly:
Local organising exists but is thin and has contracted. Bedayaa, founded in 2010, continues to serve the LGBT+ community in the Nile valley region of Sudan and Egypt. Freedom Sudan, founded in December 2006, has shown no internet presence since 2013. Rainbow Sudan, founded on 9 February 2012, provided sexual education, psychological and emotional support, and protection before ceasing its internet presence after January 2015. In 2011 there were no known LGBT organisations in the country.

Rainbow Sudan, a Sudanese community magazine, documented local community presence through sections on LGBTI rights in Sudan, including history and analysis and profiles of Sudanese LGBTI organisations.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources conflict on whether transgender-specific criminal provisions exist. One profile cites Article 152 of the Penal Code as a cross-dressing offence; an open reference source states that the only criminal offence described is sodomy under Article 148 and that no transgender-specific criminal provision is described. No arrest statistics for transgender people are available.

No transgender-specific information is sourced on document markers, screening, detention facilities, custody arrangements, or care provision beyond the absence of legal gender recognition and the legal constraints on gender-affirming healthcare.

The 2010 human rights report predates the 2020 amendment and describes the penalties then in force. Whether Article 152 is enforced against transgender visitors is not sourced.
